title: Stage 4 review: fundamentals of stock investing
subtitle: Stage 2 summary
openingQuestion: After all of Stage 4, if you had to sum up the philosophy of fundamental stock investing in one sentence, which best captures the thread running through every lesson?
openingOptions: Just follow tips from people who claim years of market experience - no need to analyze anything yourself at all
The more times you trade in a single day, the more certain your total return will be higher than trading less often
Understand what you're buying, diversify, keep discipline, and be patient
Just pick one stock rumored to be a 'super stock' and put your entire capital into it - the shortest path to getting rich fast
explanation: The whole of Stage 4 revolves around four pillars: understanding the investment tools (stocks, ETFs, open-end funds, valuation), managing risk (diversification, avoiding excess leverage), psychological discipline (avoiding greed and fear), and realistic expectations (roughly 8-12%/year long-term, not getting rich quick).

realWorldExample.company: The journey from beginner to disciplined investor
realWorldExample.description: A typical individual investor in Vietnam usually follows exactly the sequence taught in Stage 4: open a brokerage account (self-managed or through an open-end fund), learn to read P/E and basic financial statements, live through at least one sharp market swing (like the 2022 or 2025 corrections) to feel fear and greed firsthand, gradually grasp the importance of portfolio diversification, and eventually build a disciplined DCA strategy anchored to realistic return expectations rather than get-rich-quick ones.

quiz.question: In Stage 4, what's the relationship between 'realistic return expectations' and the 'common mistakes new investors make'?
options: Unrealistic expectations are the root cause behind those other mistakes
Return expectations apply only to bonds, not to stocks
The two topics are entirely separate with no notable link
These two topics have no cause-and-effect relationship at all
quiz.explanation: This is the core link running through Stage 4: when return expectations are inflated beyond reality, investors are more willing to take on excessive risk (margin, concentrating in one stock, trusting tips) to try to reach that unrealistic level.

quiz.question: How are DCA and investing psychology connected?
options: Investing psychology only affects sellers, not buyers, a point that trips up many beginners
DCA turns buying into an automatic habit run on a schedule
DCA only suits an investor with absolutely no emotions at all
The two topics are separate, with no meaningful real-world link
quiz.explanation: DCA is a practical tool for dealing with the very psychological problem covered earlier: by automating the buy decision onto a fixed schedule, an investor cuts down the room for greed or fear to control the timing of purchases.

quiz.question: How are portfolio risk and choosing an ETF/open-end fund (covered in earlier lessons) connected?
options: Open-end funds do nothing to support the goal of portfolio diversification
Portfolio risk and ETF/open-end fund tools are unrelated to each other, even when the portfolio risk in question is concentrated entirely in a single stock
ETFs and open-end funds are ready-made tools for practicing diversification
An ETF always carries higher risk than holding a single stock outright, something worth double-checking in practice
quiz.explanation: This is a clear example of how Stage 4's concepts connect to practice: the principle of diversifying to cut unsystematic risk is put into concrete practice through an ETF or open-end fund (a managed account) without having to personally manage dozens of individual stocks.

quiz.question: Of these three things, which does an individual investor control the most: market returns, investment costs, or the timing of the market bottom?
options: Market returns
Investment costs: fees, taxes, and how often the portfolio turns over each year
The timing of the market bottom
All three are equally controllable if you follow the news closely enough
quiz.explanation: Fees, taxes, and portfolio turnover are things you decide directly and can know the number of in advance. Nobody controls market returns or the timing of the bottom. That's why a good strategy always starts by cutting the losses that are certain.

quiz.question: In this stage, where do diversification and realistic return expectations reinforce each other?
options: Both reduce the chance you'll be forced to sell off your portfolio near a market bottom
Both push the portfolio's expected return up to a higher level
Both are tools for forecasting when the market will reverse direction
Both only work for an investor with large capital and a lot of free time
quiz.explanation: Diversification shrinks the size of the drawdown, and realistic expectations keep that drawdown from being outside what was anticipated. Both target an individual investor's single biggest risk: selling at the bottom out of panic - an act that destroys long-term returns more than any stock-picking mistake.

keyTakeaways: Stage 4 revolves around four tightly linked pillars: investment tools and valuation (ETFs, open-end funds, P/E), risk management (diversification, avoiding leverage), psychological discipline (avoiding greed/fear, DCA), and realistic expectations (8-12%/year long-term, not getting rich quick)
Unrealistic return expectations are the root cause of most other mistakes: excess leverage, trusting tips, trading too often
Vietnam's securities tax (0.1% of sale value) and various fees (trading, fund management) are real costs that eat into net return, though easy to overlook
Both buy and sell decisions should be based on the business's fundamentals and a plan set in advance, not on short-term price swings or a passing emotion

practicePrompt.question: A friend says: 'I read the 5 Stage-4 lessons, so now I'm going to use margin to buy one single super-stock on a tip - DCA is too slow for that.' How many of Stage 4's core principles is this friend ignoring?
options: At least three: diversification, avoiding excess leverage, and not trusting unverified tips
Only one single principle is being ignored - not using a DCA strategy when trading, a nuance that matters more than it first appears
No principle is being violated at all; this is simply a faster, more decisive investing strategy
The whole of Stage 4 revolves around just one principle - realistic return expectations - and the others don't matter
practicePrompt.explanation: This friend's plan violates three pillars of Stage 4 at once: risk management (diversification, avoiding leverage) and discipline (not trusting unverified tips).

application.title: Grade yourself on Stage 4
application.message: Write one sentence for each pillar: which investment tool you understand best, which risk-management rule you'll apply, and what your current realistic return expectation is in %/year.
application.secondary: Summarizing in your own words helps the knowledge stick far longer.

sections.text: Stage 4 has covered a fairly long journey: from the basic concepts of stocks, ETFs, and valuation, through to hands-on lessons on psychology, risk, tax, and buy/sell strategy. This lesson assembles it all into one coherent picture.
Group 1: Tools and how to value them

The early lessons of Stage 4 built the foundation of basic investment tools: stocks, ETFs, open-end funds, how to read valuation metrics like P/E and ROE, how to pick a suitable ETF (underlying assets, fees, liquidity, fund size), and how a fund's expense ratio quietly erodes returns over time.
Group 2: Buying strategy - DCA and realistic expectations

The DCA lesson introduced it as a periodic investing method that reduces the psychological risk of buying, even though it doesn't statistically guarantee a higher return than investing a lump sum at once. The next lesson followed by setting realistic return expectations - roughly 8-12%/year on average over the long run, not the 50-100%/year often told in anecdotes. Together, these two lessons build one mindset: stock investing is a patient, multi-year journey, not a get-rich-quick game.
Group 3: Psychology and mistakes to avoid

The two lessons on psychology and mistakes dug into the human side of investing: greed drives people to chase rising prices and over-leverage; fear drives people to sell off right when prices are low. From there, the common mistakes of new investors - concentrating capital in one stock, overusing margin, trusting tips, trading too often, having no clear plan - all trace back to a lack of discipline in the face of market emotion.

items: DCA and psychology: DCA is a practical tool for reducing emotion's influence on buy timing
Mistakes and expectations: unrealistic expectations are the root cause of many investing mistakes
Portfolio risk and ETFs/open-end funds: diversification is put into concrete practice through the tools already covered
Tax and overtrading: the 0.1% tax on sale value per trade makes frequent trading even more costly
When to sell and psychology: a sell decision should rest on business fundamentals, not on emotion in the face of a price swing

sections.text: Group 4: Risk, tax, and real costs

The portfolio-risk lesson distinguished systematic risk (which cannot be eliminated) from unsystematic risk (which can be reduced through diversification). The tax lesson clarified a point that's easy to confuse: Vietnam's securities tax is 0.1% of the SALE VALUE, not of the profit as with a US-style capital gains tax - and it applies even when the sale is at a loss. The following lesson expanded into the choice between managing the account yourself or letting an expert/open-end fund manage it instead, each choice trading off cost against time differently.
Group 5: When to sell and how to analyze in practice

The lesson on when to sell closed out the strategy section with a question that's often forgotten: when should you sell? The answer is consistent with the whole stage: sell because the business's fundamentals have genuinely changed, not out of panic over a short-term price swing. The stage's final lesson, through the FPT case study, assembled all the knowledge about valuation, profit trends, and dividends into a concrete process that can be applied to any stock.

sections.label: The thread running through Stage 4
sections.text: If there's one single message running through the whole stage: successful stock investing doesn't depend on finding a 'magic stock' or a 'perfect moment' - it depends on building a system - understanding the tools, diversifying risk, keeping emotional discipline, holding realistic expectations, and having a clear plan for both buying and selling - then sticking to that system for years.

lines: Stage 4 doesn't close with a get-rich formula, but with a way of thinking: know your tools, manage risk, stay disciplined, and be patient over time.
This knowledge only has real value when applied consistently over many years - not read once and forgotten.
